quote: I would nominate, as the basic error not to repeat next time, that the early scientists forgot that they themselves were made out of particles.
content: They did not forget; they calculated. Mott in 1929 treated the cloud chamber’s atoms quantum-mechanically to explain straight tracks (Mott (1929)); von Neumann in 1932 applied the unitary dynamics to the apparatus and the observer’s nervous system, showed the chain terminates nowhere, and concluded that a second process was needed to get the definite outcomes that were seen; Bohr’s insistence on a classical description of the apparatus was a doctrine about the conditions of unambiguous communication, argued at length, not an oversight. What the essay describes as the missing insight, that the sensor and the brain are “particles in different places,” is the content of the von Neumann chain, and the conclusion those physicists drew from it was that applying the laws to themselves does not yield a single result, which is the measurement problem. The essay’s moral, that they should have applied the laws to themselves, is a description of what they did; the disagreement is over what to conclude when the application leaves the observed definiteness unexplained. The sequence’s answer is that the definiteness is an artefact of decoherence plus a Born measure it cannot derive, and “they forgot they were made of particles” is a way of not saying that.

quote: And yet it wasn’t professional philosophers who swooped in and solved the problem and cleared up the mystery and made everything normal again. It was, well, physicists.
content: The interpretation the essay is endorsing was, in its modern form, largely built by philosophers. The decoherence-based Everett programme that treats worlds as emergent structure, supplies the decision-theoretic account of probability, and defends the view against the preferred-basis objection is the work of the Oxford school, Saunders, Wallace, Greaves and Deutsch, of whom three are philosophers by department and training, and its canonical statement is a philosophy book (Wallace, The Emergent Multiverse, 2012). The objections that keep it honest come from philosophers too (Albert, Maudlin, Kent’s co-authors). Bell, who did more than anyone to make the foundations respectable, described his own work as philosophy and was answering Bohm and EPR, which were philosophical arguments. The claim that professional philosophy of physics is “a mistake,” like having separate ethicists, is made in a sequence whose every substantive move (the conceivability–possibility distinction, the status of the Born rule, the emergence of worlds, the meaning of locality) is a move philosophers of physics made first and are still making. The essay’s advice that philosophers should learn the science is sound; the ones it is dismissing did.
